theme: Doctrinal Pause: Death and the Intermediate State
summary: What happens at death; the conscious presence of believers with Christ; the soul-body distinction
readingInstruction: Read 2 Corinthians 5:1-10, Philippians 1:21-24, and Luke 23:39-43. Today is a doctrinal pause on death and the intermediate state, the time between a believer’s death and the resurrection. Notice what Paul expects and what Jesus promises.
settingTheScene: Yesterday and the day before, we studied the resurrection of the dead at the end of the age. But what happens to believers who die before Christ returns? Paul was facing possible death in Asia, and in Philippians he wrote from prison, aware that he might be executed. Their words, along with Jesus’ promise to the thief on the cross, tell us what the New Testament says about the time between death and resurrection.
observation: “For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).
“For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7).
“We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8).
“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10).
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).
“My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23).
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43).
doctrinalFocus:
The intermediate state is the condition of a person between death and the resurrection of the body. Scripture teaches that when a believer dies, the person is immediately with Christ, in conscious fellowship and joy, although without a resurrection body. Paul says to be “away from the body” is to be “at home with the Lord.” He says that departing is “far better” than staying. Jesus told the penitent thief, “Today you will be with me in Paradise.” This is the common evangelical understanding, and it is a great comfort.

This state is not the final one. Paul pictures it as being “unclothed” (2 Corinthians 5:3-4), awaiting the “clothing” of the resurrection body. The final hope remains the resurrection and the new creation. The intermediate state is a waiting period, but it is a good one, in the presence of Christ.

Several other views exist. Some Christians hold to “soul sleep,” the idea that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. The language of “sleep” in the New Testament describes how death looks from our side, but passages like Philippians 1 and Luke 23 point to conscious fellowship. The Roman Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a place of purification after death for those who die in grace but not fully cleansed. Protestants reject this because Christ’s work on the cross is sufficient, and Scripture speaks of immediate presence with Christ. Other traditions emphasize that God’s people await the resurrection, stressing the whole person.

For unbelievers, the New Testament speaks of a state of waiting for judgment, with the final judgment to come (Luke 16:19-31; Hebrews 9:27). All will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. For believers, this is not a judgment about our standing, which is secure in Christ, but about our works, for reward. The thought of that day motivates faithful service.
interpretation:
Paul begins 2 Corinthians 5 with a contrast between the earthly tent and the eternal building. A tent is temporary; our bodies are like tents, vulnerable and short-lived. If the tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” In the meantime, “we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling.” He does not want to be unclothed but further clothed, “so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” God has prepared us for this and given us the Spirit as a guarantee.

“So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight. Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.” To be “at home with the Lord” is the heart of the intermediate state. Whether at home or away, our aim is to please him, “for we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.” For the believer, this is a day for evaluation and reward, not condemnation (Romans 8:1).

In Philippians 1, Paul is in prison, uncertain whether he will live or die. He writes, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” He is hard-pressed between the two: “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.” Notice his confidence: death does not end fellowship with Christ; it increases it. The word “depart” was used of a ship loosing its moorings or a tent being taken down.

In Luke 23, one of the criminals crucified with Jesus rebukes the other, acknowledges his own guilt, and says, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” He had no time for baptism, good works, or a long spiritual track record. Jesus answers with a promise: “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise.” Salvation by grace through faith, and immediate presence with Christ, in one scene. “Today.” The thief received what Paul described.

Death is still an enemy, and Christians grieve. But it has lost its sting, and it is the doorway to being with Christ.
connection: Psalm 23:4 speaks of walking through the valley of the shadow of death. Psalm 116:15 says the death of his saints is precious. Ecclesiastes 12:7 speaks of the spirit returning to God. Luke 16:19-31 tells of the rich man and Lazarus. John 14:1-3 promises a place with him. Acts 7:59 records Stephen’s prayer, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Hebrews 12:22-24 mentions the spirits of the righteous made perfect. Revelation 6:9-11 shows souls under the altar. 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 comforts the grieving. Romans 14:7-9 says whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
application:
Write down what you believe about what happens when a Christian dies. Compare it to these passages.

Pray for someone who is facing death or grief. Share Philippians 1:21 with them.

Ask what it would mean to say, “To me to live is Christ,” in your daily work.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you think about death today.
Thank Jesus that to live is Christ and to die is gain.
Thank him that to be away from the body is to be at home with him.
